summary: Pablo Castro frames his talk around three categories of knowledge: intrinsic, extrinsic, and learned. Intrinsic knowledge refers to what models store in parametric memory from training data, which Castro argues launched the current AI exponential. He illustrates this through coding tool evolution: IntelliSense (1996) took 22 years to advance to ML-ranked suggestions, then just 3 more years to GitHub Copilot, followed by rapid succession of Cursor, Copilot X, Opus 4.5, and AI-generated software like Open Claw with no hand-written code. Microsoft supports this through its agent platform spanning GitHub for building, Foundry for hosting and observability, and a model catalog with thousands of models including newly GA Claude. Castro then addresses extrinsic knowledge, noting intrinsic models alone cannot support organizational agents. He describes the evolution from simple RAG to sophisticated context engineering, highlighting two complexity dimensions: company-wide grounding and retrieval system sophistication. Microsoft IQ provides a unified entry point across Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ. On retrieval, Castro explains that combined methods consistently outperform individual methods in Azure AI Search evaluations. Foundry IQ's layered design lets users start simple or dive deep into expert controls, with agentic retrieval for complex queries. The system is also designed for token efficiency, delivering information-dense answers with minimal tokens. The Foundry IQ demo shows creating a knowledge base with movie data combining unstructured, structured, and web sources, each functioning as an MCP server. Castro then introduces learned knowledge—the result of organizational processes that agents can observe and improve through reflection. He references Satya Nadella's writing on people and agents compounding through learning loops that capture organizational differentiation. The Foundry agent optimizer materializes this: it evaluates a baseline agent, generates candidate configurations, hill-climbs the evaluation metric, and deploys improved configurations. The VS Code demo shows eval generation for task adherence, optimization producing non-handwritten instructions that emerge from the process, and one-click application of optimized configs. Castro closes by directing listeners to ai.azure.com.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Intrinsic Knowledge
sections.summary: Castro introduces his role connecting AI and knowledge at Microsoft, then defines three knowledge categories: intrinsic, extrinsic, and learned. Intrinsic knowledge is the parametric memory from training data that launched the current AI exponential.

sections.title: AI Coding Tool Evolution
sections.summary: Castro traces coding tool evolution: IntelliSense (1996), ML-ranked suggestions (22 years later), GitHub Copilot (3 years after that, before ChatGPT), then Cursor, Copilot X, Opus 4.5, and Open Claw with no hand-written code—illustrating the exponential driven by intrinsic model knowledge and reasoning ability.

sections.title: Microsoft Agent Platform and Model Catalog
sections.summary: Microsoft's agent platform spans GitHub for building with contextualization, Foundry for hosting/observability/management, and a model catalog with thousands of models. Claude in Microsoft Foundry announced as generally available.

sections.title: Extrinsic Knowledge and Company Grounding
sections.summary: Intrinsic models alone cannot support organizational agents. RAG evolved from low-tech to sophisticated context engineering. Microsoft IQ provides unified access to ambient organizational data: Work IQ (SharePoint, emails, calendar, chats), Fabric IQ (analytics, Power BI), Foundry IQ (custom agent data), and Web IQ (public information).

sections.title: Retrieval System Evolution and Foundry IQ Architecture
sections.summary: Vector databases initially unblocked RAG but combined retrieval methods consistently outperform individual methods. Foundry IQ uses layered design: auto chunking/vectorization/ranking at top, expert controls (quantization, vector algorithms, lexical retrieval) at bottom. Agentic retrieval stack enables systems to reflect on datasets and verify information needs before returning results.

sections.title: Foundry IQ Demo: Knowledge Base Creation
sections.summary: Live demo creates a Foundry knowledge base with movie data, configuring agentic retrieval with model and effort settings. Combines unstructured PDFs from blob storage, structured parquet tables, and web sources. Knowledge base connects to Foundry agents and functions as standalone MCP server. Azure portal demo shows backing indexes, structure, quantization options, and data exploration.

sections.title: Token Efficiency and Learned Knowledge
sections.summary: Castro emphasizes token efficiency in Foundry IQ retrieval, delivering information-dense answers with minimal tokens. He then introduces learned knowledge as the third category: the result of organizational processes that agents can observe and improve through reflection. He references Satya Nadella's writing on people and agents compounding through learning loops that capture organizational differentiation. Foundry offers the agent optimizer as a materialized learning loop that evaluates a baseline, generates candidates, and deploys optimized configurations.

sections.title: Foundry Agent Optimizer Demo
sections.summary: VS Code demo with Foundry toolkit shows a simple agent with externalized configuration. Two key steps: eval generate produces task adherence evaluation from traces and instructions, then optimize runs hill climbing on the evaluation metric for approximately 45 minutes. Results show baseline vs. optimized candidates using different combinations in a J-power style loop. Applying the optimized configuration swaps in non-handwritten instructions that emerged from the hill climbing process, reflecting actual agent usage traces—materializing a real learning loop in practice.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Castro recaps the three knowledge categories and how learning loops capture differentiated organizational capabilities. He directs listeners to ai.azure.com to try the tools and thanks the audience.

demonstrations: Foundry IQ demo: Creating a knowledge base from movie dataset with agentic retrieval, configuring model and effort level, combining unstructured PDFs from blob storage, structured parquet tables, and web sources
Azure portal demo: Inspecting knowledge base internals—viewing backing indexes, index structure, quantization approach options, vector indexing algorithms, chunk organization, and data exploration

Foundry agent optimizer demo: In VS Code with Foundry toolkit, running eval generate to produce task adherence evaluation from agent traces, running optimize (approximately 45 minutes) to hill-climb the evaluation metric, viewing baseline vs optimized candidate results, and applying optimized configuration with non-handwritten instructions that emerged from the optimization process
limitations: Intrinsic model knowledge only gets you so far when building agents that need to participate in organizational workflows
Simple vector search and cosine similarity alone proved insufficient for real-world retrieval scenarios
Individual retrieval methods underperform compared to combined methods in real-world customer scenarios
Single-shot retrieval is inadequate for sophisticated cases requiring reflection on dataset completeness
